text: At the end of its mission, Cassini had so little fuel that it could drift into a moon by accident. The chosen solution was a controlled plunge into Saturn, where the atmosphere would tear it apart rather than risk it hitting Enceladus or Titan. That matters because those moons are thought to have liquid subsurface oceans and might harbor life, so bringing Earth microbes or space debris down onto them could mess with any biosignatures. Leaving it in orbit was not really an option; a slow uncontrolled decay would eventually send it somewhere dangerous. In practice, the dive protected the moons while giving the spacecraft a clean ending.

The fact that it's the stationary leg that aches is actually normal. Your body has to control a moving board with one foot anchored. The muscle in that leg stays braced and tense while the other foot shifts; that continuous low-level holding is what gives you the dull ache, not some fresh injury. In my experience this is what most people get when they skate for longer than usual, or when they don't take breaks, and it usually fades after a day or two of rest and light stretching. What matters for your case is that you should look at your stance before assuming anything is wrong with the leg itself. If your weight is loading the stationary leg hard to keep the board steady, that leg is doing more work than it should, which explains why the discomfort is tied to riding. I'd ride with a more balanced stance and take a break if the ache builds, rather than pushing through it. If the pain is sharp, localized to one spot, or still there after a day off, that's when it deserves a check with a physio or doctor. For now, I'd treat it as overuse rather than a structural problem; a slow walk, some gentle calf and thigh stretches, and shorter sessions should settle it. Watch it for a day or two. If it only shows up with the leg bent or loaded the same way every time, and rest doesn't take it away, then a simple assessment is worth doing. I wouldn't jump to a bad knee or bad hip over one dull complaint. The key is to stop treating the leg as the problem and adjust how you hold your weight on the board.

I get the confusion. The term isn't being used because those people currently came from the African continent. It's an ancestral label, not a statement about where someone just moved from. In American usage since at least the 18th century, it identifies a group by its origins in Africa through forced migration. The word was applied to people of African descent living in America, regardless of whether their direct ancestors ever set foot in Africa. Most of them were born in the US, or their parents were; that doesn't change the ancestry. For you, if the question is about the mismatch between the name and where people actually live or were born, that's the exact distinction: lineage, not passport. I'd treat 'Afro-American' the same way you'd treat 'Iroquois' or 'Japanese American', a heritage label rather than a migration statement. One caveat: people sometimes overreach and use it as if everyone must have personally been in Africa recently. If you're explaining it to someone, stick to the lineage angle. The term does carry an assumption of continental origin, which is fair but easily stretched too far. No need to turn it into an encyclopedia entry. Just say it names ancestry, not residence.

That's mostly border trade, not factory output. Small arms move across the frontiers with Iraq, Jordan, Turkey, Lebanon, and Israel; bigger items come through the same channels or fall out of state depots after the regime changes hands. That's why they still get them: local economies and armed groups need guns, and the supply lines are older and more robust than most outsiders expect, with informal markets doing the moving. I'd say the demand outlasts the supply restrictions, so expect more of this. The routes are old, and nobody is closing all of them at once.

Yeah, I think you're noticing a very real problem, but I wouldn't let "all drugs are bad" stick, because it flattens a lot of medicine into the same pile. The complaint is really about the recreational stuff: heroine, coke, amphetamine, MDMA, the ones with strong euphoria. Those are the ones people chase for the feeling, and that's exactly why they carry risks.

What's happening is the body trying to keep its baseline. A drug that drives mood that far off that baseline triggers counter-regulation. Heroine and coke push the reward system, and the system pulls back. You get tolerance, the original high fades, you chase more, and dependence sets in. It is the same reward machinery creating the high and the correction. That extra cost is built into the balance mechanism, so you cannot have intense pleasure and zero adverse effects at the same time without changing how the brain compensates.

Could there be a drug with intense pleasure and zero adverse effects? In principle, maybe; in practice, it's hard. If it really did have zero adverse effects, the brain might not mount much counter-regulation, so tolerance would develop slowly or not at all. But if you avoid that counter-regulation, you usually can't get the huge peak you want. Pushing strongly past normal reward signalling makes the body correct, and that correction shows up as loss of feeling, withdrawal, needing more.

I'd also separate "bad" from "risky". Some drugs are benign for many people. Caffeine gives a tiny lift and, for many, no big problems. But heroine, coke, and similar strong mood-stimulating drugs are another story. The stronger the reward effect, the more likely the system pushes back.

A milder drug could exist, something that lifts mood only gently. But you asked for intense pleasure, and that's where the body's correction becomes harder to avoid. Most recreational highs fit this pattern because they work on the same reward circuits, whether you're talking about heroine, coke, or the other substances in your "etc". If someone claims their drug avoids the cost, I'd ask how the reward system compensates. If the answer is simply that the body never adapts, then I'd suspect the peak is milder too. A zero-adverse-effect drug is a theoretical possibility, but the intense-euphoria drugs we know still carry the costs you're pointing at.

Hi,

You're not imagining it. It's real, not just in your head and I get it. A long day with your wife taxes the body in ways that don't show as a usual headache. I think it's mainly accumulated fatigue, poor hydration and the mental load of constantly choosing, comparing and saying no. Since she is moving and so are you, and you keep being dragged into every judgment, it ends up worse than a headache. Next time stop for water and eat when hungry; don't get pulled into every decision. If the pain keeps happening, get it checked.

Thanks

Hi,

Your brother is running a little trick on you, not checking how smart you are. The silk-and-spelling bit gets you stuck in the letter pattern of "silk", and then the cow question lands while your attention is still fixed on that pattern. So instead of answering with water, the most obvious associated word, milk, just comes out. It is a bit unfair, but that's exactly the point: he is testing whether the association can take over while you are distracted. The fact that cows actually drink water does not matter as much as the fact that milk is the culturally automatic answer for cows, and that's what came out for you. If you were concentrating on spelling silk, your brain had less spare capacity to second-guess the easy answer. If he asks again, say water with a straight face. He is using a well-worn trick, and you fell for it.

Thanks

Hi,

Buying a home is more about cash flow and risk than romance. First, figure out what you can actually afford without maxing yourself out. A mortgage that leaves you only a little room for rates, insurance, taxes and repairs will become stressful fast. I would build a budget with a margin for emergencies, because houses are not passive. A second checkup matters too: look at roof, wiring, plumbing, water pressure, drainage and the age of major systems, and if anything seems off, pay for a professional inspection. Don’t skip the survey or the title search; they’re the parts that save money later.

If you’re worried about value or financing, talk to a mortgage adviser and a local agent. Get written quotes for a lender, and compare the total monthly payment, not just the advertised interest. Also ask the seller for service history and any known problems, and don’t ignore the parking and commute, which often decide a neighbourhood’s value too. One more point: don’t let an open offer or a falling house price tempt you into overstretching. Buying a home is a long-term commitment, so make sure the numbers leave you a buffer, not just the smallest payment.

Thanks

Hi,

I've used these a few times, and the difference is not really a mystery. A separate bodywash and separate shampoo are not just mixed together in a bottle; a 3-in-1 has to be mild enough for skin while also lifting hair, so makers usually choose softer, multi-purpose surfactants. That is the key point: the detergent system is built to do both jobs, not one strong cleanser plus a separate treatment.

Because of that, the conditioner part is often very thin. A 2-in-1 at least separates hair-washing from body washing, but still has one formula doing two things. A 3-in-1 extends that to skin. For most people with normal hair, it is convenient and fine for a quick trip. If your hair is curly, colored, or damaged, you will probably be better off with dedicated products, because the formula cannot give the stronger cleansing or heavier conditioning those types need.

The other thing worth knowing: these can feel slick, but that is not the same as real conditioning. I would not rely on it as a daily main product unless you specifically want one bottle for everything.

Thanks

Hi,

Your continent isn't drifting like a boat; it's shifting a few centimeters per year, and that can be measured directly. They use a network of GPS receivers on the continent. Each station records where it is from satellite signals, and when you compare its position at one time against the same station later, the small change is the drift. Repeat that over months or years and the speed is clear. You don't need to watch the land move; the satellites and the network do the math for you. The reference frame matters: ITRF and plate-fixed velocities don't always agree. A station's numbers only make sense once the frame is named. For older continental motion, rock and fossil records show much bigger rearrangement over geological time. That part can't be measured by GPS alone. I'd keep both together: GPS tells current plate velocity, geology tells past motion. The method is precise at centimeter scale, though local tectonic adjustments can make one station look odd. This is why one station can disagree with its neighbours. In practice, if someone asks how fast a continent is moving, check a published tectonic plate model or GPS velocity field rather than one station's quirks. I'd treat the centimeters/year figures as a regional range, not one station's quirks.

Thanks

If two related people have children, their baby is more likely to inherit the same rare harmful genetic variants on both copies of the same genes. That is the core issue. Many small differences in cognitive ability are controlled by lots of genes, and harmful variants often act recessively: one copy hides, two copies show up. Close relatives share much of their DNA, so the chance that both parents carry the same damaging variant is higher than in unrelated couples. That does not mean inbreeding lowers IQ in a single child every time; it raises the risk and the population average drops.

For our wiki, the practical point is that inbreeding reduces genetic diversity in families and makes hidden problems more visible. The effect is not about intelligence itself being “diluted”; it is about the load of harmful variants becoming homozygous and affecting traits like cognition. It’s the same idea as a recessive condition.

Pain is not evenly distributed across the body. Whether an injury hurts depends on the tissue damaged, the nerves involved, and how the brain interprets the signal. An arm injury may seem less painful than an injury to the torso or leg partly because the arm is a peripheral appendage, and the brain can mentally distance it from your central self.

The body does not, however, have a special pain switch in the arm. The forearm and hand contain many sensitive nerve endings, so a cut near the wrist can still sting badly. For a new colleague, the practical point is: don't assume arm pain is automatically mild. A sharp or burning pain, numbness, or weakness in the arm may suggest nerve, tendon, or vascular involvement and needs medical assessment. If the injury is a hit, shot, or stab, also watch for movement limits and bleeding if it doesn't improve.

It comes down to how oxygen gets around in your blood. Your red blood cells carry oxygen using a protein called hemoglobin. Carbon monoxide binds to that hemoglobin roughly two hundred times tighter than oxygen does, so it locks out the oxygen and your organs start starving. Carbon dioxide is just the normal waste gas your cells produce, and your lungs are specifically built to exhale it, so it does not trap oxygen the same way.

For our offices and facilities, this means we have to treat CO as a serious, silent hazard, especially in enclosed spaces, parking structures, or anywhere we run generators or heaters. Because it is colorless, odorless, and tastes like nothing, you will not know it is there until you feel dizzy, get a headache, or worse. That is why the safety team installs those small rectangular detectors in the basements, mechanical rooms, and near the boiler heaters.

I think we need to be stricter about maintaining them. I want the facilities crew to check and log the battery expiry dates on all the units in the building maintenance tracker next month, because a dead battery in the boiler room is just a bad day waiting to happen. If a detector beeps, the rule is to clear the room immediately and find the source. High CO2 levels can make a room feel stuffy and cause brain fog, which is why we use those sensors for basic ventilation control, but you are not going to suffocate from normal indoor air. CO is the one that stops your delivery system. Keep the detectors powered, test them on schedule, and make sure everyone on the new hire orientation knows what to do when a gas alarm sounds.

You’re much safer if you enter the brace position early in an aircraft emergency. It won’t make the crash feel comfortable, but it changes how impact forces move through your body. With feet flat on the floor, torso leaned forward, and hands over your head, your body is less likely to be thrown forward or upward. That is what the position is for. It gives you a stable base and keeps you from hitting seat backs, floor, or overhead bins.

The crew may ask you to sit flat, grab your ankles if you can, protect your head, and stay low. If they announce an imminent hard landing, do it quickly. The brace makes your skeleton carry the main load, while your organs stop moving freely inside your ribcage. This is why the seatbelt card demonstration looks uncomfortable: it is not posture for comfort, it is protection for the next few seconds.

If you are in a narrow-aisle seat, keep your legs off the floor when the aircraft settles. If you have a window, do not fight out of the position after the crew have ordered it. The practical point is that braces work best when done early, and without hesitation.

That's a fair question, and the core reason is scale. Before the steam engine, railroads, and modern packaging, moving heavy goods across oceans was so slow and expensive that a company could only survive by making the most of a single local market. The few pre-industrial exceptions that are still around are mostly Japanese trading houses or old European banks, which were built around credit rather than shipping bricks. I'd bet most of those old firms had to completely reinvent their core model when freight got cheap and reliable, or they just went under. It's not that older firms didn't exist; it's that their models broke once shipping costs crashed.

I keep thinking about why the bank can beat the dealership despite lower dealer rates. Last time I bought a car, I used the bank, not the dealer's financing office, and the reason was not subtle. Dealerships often package the money so the sticker rate looks great while the rest of the cost hides in the paperwork. In my case, the advertised rate was a teaser for a short term. It looked cheap until I added the large payment due at the end and the dealer fees. The bank's rate was higher, but the loan ran longer and did not add a forced payoff. When I totaled what I would actually pay, the bank came out cheaper. That is why I went with it, even though the dealership's rate was lower.

The annoying part is that the advertised number makes the dealer's offer look better on paper. People get stuck comparing monthly payments, which is where dealers like you to focus. I stop looking at the sticker rate and ask for the full payment schedule. I look for fees, term length, any large payment due later, and how much I would owe in total. If the dealer is using its credit company, there can be a markup in the interest rate that never shows up on the sticker. Banks may look less generous because they do not have a sales floor pushing a payment, but their paperwork is usually simpler.

This is not to say dealerships are always worse. If the bank is the only option, or if the car is new and the dealer's low rate is a genuine promotional offer without a forced payoff, the dealer can be the cheaper route. But more often than not, the low rate comes with short terms and fee stacks that quietly erase the savings.

What I do now is write down the total cost before signing. I do not let a 0% or 1% headline fool me. I ask for the loan schedule and out-of-pocket fees, then do the math. If a short term and a balloon payment are part of the offer, I compare the bank's longer loan instead. That is how I ended up paying less, even though the dealership had the lower advertised rate. The rate is one line in the costs list, and the dealer sells you the list, not just the rate.

Marijuana is still treated as a class C felony in four US states, while the other forty-six have legalized it in some form, so the word “legal” hides a huge gap. I’d argue the country is moving toward state freedom with clear rules, not toward a single national rule. Each state can decide what its residents can use and sell, but it needs published thresholds, tax rates, licensing conditions, and enforcement guidelines. That level of detail matters more than a simple legal or illegal label. My position is that states should keep deciding, but they should make their rules easier for businesses and users to understand. A patchwork only works when the differences are explicit and documented. That is how I see this.

I used to think the body was exactly like a tiny battery, but really it isn't. It's closer to a nervous system managing ions across cell membranes. Sodium-potassium pumps push potassium in and sodium out, and that difference in charge is what makes a neuron's membrane polarized. When a signal starts, sodium channels open, ions rush in, and that brief spike is the electricity your nerves carry. That's not some abstract biochemistry; it's how your brain fires, your muscles twitch, your heart keeps a rhythm. In short, the body's electricity is ion chemistry working quietly to keep you alive.

I think the least sexy part of sampling is the paperwork. Musicians can pull a drum break out of a 1975 record and loop it in a DAW, but if the sample is recognizable in a released track, they are dealing with rights. In practice, that means identifying the writer and the recording owner, then negotiating a license or a buyout. A short rhythmic fragment may not get noticed, but the moment it becomes a distinctive hook, it can become a legal issue.

I like sampling as a way of putting an old song in a new body. You cut the section you want, usually a few seconds, then stretch or shorten it, change the pitch, add bass, clean up the vinyl crackle, and lay a fresh drum pattern around it. The old groove becomes the foundation, not a quotation. This is where the music gets interesting, because the sample gives you a character that a synth or live drum take might not. But the character is still borrowed, which is why the clearance conversation is so unglamorous.

My position is straightforward: sample what the older song did best, and stop defending the choice. If you are taking a vocal line, it is a vocal line, not a mysterious texture. If you are taking the snare hits, they are the point of the track. The best samplers, in my view, know when to leave the original almost untouched and when to bend it until it fits their song. I would rather see a producer strip away most of the source material and build something new than stack layers and hide the original.

There is also a practical question of whether a sample is long enough or distinctive enough to require clearance. A short percussive hit may be de minimis in some cases, but that is a judgment call, not a guarantee. For a commercial release, the safe route is to ask for permission from both the copyright owner of the composition and the owner of the sound recording. If those are different people, there is more red tape, not less.

This is why I don't see sampling as a shortcut. It is a craft choice that carries a cost and a creative risk. The older song gives you a starting point, but it does not make the new song, and the paperwork reminds the producer that the original has an owner.

You don’t actually get the pain from your skull or the tissue inside it, because most of the head is quite insensitive on its own. What matters is the blood vessels and the membranes under the bone (the stuff that wraps around the brain and holds it in place), because those are packed with pain fibres. So the head hurts when something makes those membranes stretch or become inflamed, or when a vessel tightens, not because your head is somehow ‘broken.’ In my case, the trigger has been the usual boring things: not enough sleep, not enough water, and the stress that keeps me from either of those. My head doesn’t hurt for no reason; it hurts when that alarm system gets set off. That’s why a bad one often comes with a pounding near the temples, because that’s where those sensitive vessels and membranes sit close to the surface.

We can't tell if the food is good; we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. Sunday and picked the place because of our 10:00 p.m. show in the same hotel, so it should have been easy. They had us use their completely useless digital waitlist, then told us to come back to pay at 8:23 p.m. We actually paid, then stood around until 8:40 p.m. before staff casually mentioned we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15 p.m. Just a party of two, yet they offered zero solutions. If the wait runs that far past payment, just say it upfront so that our night isn't completely wasted. Absolute disaster. If zero stars were an option, I'd choose zero stars.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and I was a little surprised by how empty it was because there was no line at all that day. For the two of us it came out to about $130, which I thought was pretty steep. Before going I had figured the price would be something like a steakhouse. Afterward I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I'd expected to pay at one.

No steak was offered, which disappointed me a little because at that price I assumed there would be some kind of steak option. There was lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were interesting. There were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs. The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive; it reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

Overall I'd call the buffet acceptable, but quite overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

I’ve been going to Vegas pretty much my whole life, the under-21 version, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is really smart. You look down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too. The strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers; those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not a rip-off exactly, just that if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats with maybe more clarity.

Clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle, where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal. $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was blown away either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear by telephone. They never arrived because the sales representative recorded the delivery address incorrectly. Her handwritten “7” was interpreted as a “1.” The intended address was 5407, but the shirts went to 5401. The residents there took the package to the local UPS store to be sent back, but it disappeared and was never seen or heard from again. We did not learn until several weeks later. During the dispute, we placed an extra order for two shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner handled that part. He admitted the shipment had gone to the wrong address but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He said we were partly at fault for not being friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and in the end received a credit.
